# SK2042 — The hash code reads state that equality ignores

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`GetHashCode` reads an instance member that none of the type's `Equals` methods compares, so two instances the type calls equal can hash differently.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |

## Why

The hash code contract runs in one direction only: equal objects must hash the same. A hash computed over a member that equality ignores breaks it head-on — two objects differing only in that member are equal and land in different buckets, so the second one inserted into a dictionary hides neither and finds neither, `Remove` returns `false` while `Count` still counts it, and a freshly built key never matches the entry it names. ⚠ **The reverse direction is not a defect and is deliberately not reported.** An `Equals` that compares more members than the hash reads only makes the hash weaker: every equal pair still hashes the same, which is all the contract asks. That direction is a collision-quality observation, and shipping it as a correctness finding would be one more rule that is usually right.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Order {
    public int Id { get; init; }

    public string Customer { get; init; } = "";

    public override bool Equals(object? other) => other is Order order && order.Id == Id;

    public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(Id, Customer);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Order {
    public int Id { get; init; }

    public string Customer { get; init; } = "";

    public override bool Equals(object? other) => other is Order order && order.Id == Id;

    public override int GetHashCode() => Id.GetHashCode();
}
```

## When it does not fire

The type must declare both `GetHashCode()` and at least one `Equals`, all of them with bodies in the one file that declares the type, and must not be a record — a partial type withdraws rather than being examined from one half. ⚠ **An equality set that comes back empty withdraws the type**: an `Equals` that reads no member of its own type is comparing identity, returning a constant or delegating to `base`, and treating "compares nothing" as the equality set would turn every hashed member into a finding. ⚠ **A call, in either body, to a method this type declares that is not one of its own equality members withdraws the type entirely.** A helper the analysis cannot read produces an *under*-counted equality set, and an under-counted equality set is precisely what reports a member the type does compare — the one wrong answer this rule must not give. Local functions and lambdas inside the bodies are read, because they are in the body. A property and the single field its getter returns are one piece of state, and so are an auto-property and its backing field; without that the rule would report every hand-written property in the repository. `nameof(x)` names a member and reads nothing, so it is not a read. One finding per member, reported on the member's mention in the hash. ⚠ **Mutability is not this rule's question**: a hashed member that equality *does* compare is `SK2043`'s finding, and the two partition the hashed members between them by construction rather than by filtering each other's output. Fixless — dropping the member from the hash and adding it to `Equals` are both one edit, they are opposite decisions about what the type means, and no signal in the code says which was intended. ⚠ **A type whose base list did not bind is withdrawn, and that was found by measuring rather than by reading.** On the reference trees a class declaring `IEquatable<Self>` was reported for not implementing it: without the SDK's implicit global usings the name bound to an *error* type, so the interface list held `IEquatable<>` and the comparison against `System.IEquatable`1` failed. Skala loads a compilation three ways and two of them can be incomplete, so an error type among a type's bases or interfaces now withdraws it from every rule in this batch — the same discipline `SK7080` uses for an inheritance chain it cannot walk.
